title: Left brain right brain test: which side is dominant? Free quiz — cv.cm
description: Free left brain vs right brain test: rate 14 statements to see whether your thinking style leans analytical and logical or creative and intuitive, and why the brain-dominance idea is a myth. No sign-up.
lede: Do you make lists and plans, or follow hunches and pictures? Rate 14 statements to see whether your thinking style leans analytical (the classic "left brain") or intuitive and creative ("right brain").
about: The two halves of the brain do specialize in some things: for most people, language is handled mainly on the left, and some aspects of attention, faces and spatial skills more on the right. In the 1960s Roger Sperry's split-brain studies, which later won a Nobel Prize, showed this specialization, and popular books turned it into the idea that each person is either a logical left-brain type or a creative right-brain type. That part is a myth: a 2013 University of Utah study of over 1,000 brain scans found no sign that people use one side more than the other, and creative and logical work both draw on both halves.

So this quiz does not measure your brain. It measures your thinking style, the everyday preference that the left-brain and right-brain labels were trying to describe: step-by-step, verbal and analytical, or big-picture, visual and intuitive. The statements were written for cv.cm and half of them describe the analytical side, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. Neither style is better, and most people use both.

faq.q: Is the left brain right brain theory true?
faq.a: Only partly. The hemispheres specialize in some tasks, but people are not left-brained or right-brained. Brain scans show that both sides work together on almost everything, including math and art.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and the analytical ones are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less leans analytical, 19 to 37 is balanced and 38 or more leans intuitive.
In popular use: logic, order, language, numbers, details and planning. "Right-brain" traits are imagination, intuition, images, music, emotion and the big picture.

faq.q: Can I change my thinking style?
faq.a: Yes. Styles are habits, not wiring. Analytical thinkers can practice brainstorming and sketching; intuitive thinkers can practice checklists and breaking problems into steps.

items: I often get a gut feeling about the answer before I can explain it.
I like to solve problems one logical step at a time.
I think in pictures more than in words.
I prefer clear instructions to working it out as I go.
I notice the overall mood of a place before the details.
I enjoy numbers, puzzles and logic games.
When I learn something, I want to see the big picture first.
I'm good at spotting small mistakes in writing or numbers.
I often lose track of time when I'm doing something creative.
I make lists and plans before I start something.
I'd rather improvise than follow a recipe exactly.
I usually explain my ideas better in words than with drawings.
I make decisions based on how they feel, then find the reasons.
I like to analyze the pros and cons before deciding.

left.name: Analytical thinker ("left brain", 0–18)
left.body: You lean toward logic, order and detail: you like to understand things step by step, plan before you act and check the facts. That makes you reliable with numbers, language and complex problems. Your brain isn't lopsided, though; it's a habit of thinking. Try leaving some room for hunches and sketches too, especially when a problem has no single right answer.

balanced.name: Balanced thinker (19–37)
balanced.body: You switch between analysis and intuition without much effort: you can follow a plan and still notice the bigger picture, or trust a hunch and then check it. That flexibility is what most real problems need. Notice which mode you reach for under pressure, and lean on the other when you get stuck.

right.name: Intuitive thinker ("right brain", 38–56)
right.body: You lean toward images, feelings and the big picture: you often know the answer before you can explain it, and creative work absorbs you. That helps with ideas, design and reading people. Your brain uses both halves like everyone's; this is a style. Checklists and breaking work into steps can help you finish what your imagination starts.
